recent_posts.title: How do developers define their worth when code is written by AI?
recent_posts.summary: A reflection on what defines developers in an era where AI writes code. The core argument is that being a developer was never about writing code itself, but about solving problems. Code is just a tool, and developers who embrace change and love problem-solving will continue to thrive. AI can handle the typing and releasing, but developers retain the ability to understand, improve, and direct what machines produce.

recent_posts.title: AI social media automation is replacing genuine human presence online
recent_posts.summary: A developer relations professional reflects on the rise of AI-powered social media automation tools that mimic a person's voice to post and comment on their behalf. The author argues this strips away the human and social elements that made social media valuable, drawing on personal experience running a 200k+ newsletter and podcast. The post criticizes the trend of using AI to manufacture a social presence, comparing it to sending a body double to public appearances, and urges people to only show up online when they genuinely can.

recent_posts.title: LinkedIn should penalize comment-bait engagement spam
recent_posts.summary: A critique of the 'comment X to get access' engagement-bait pattern spreading across LinkedIn and other social platforms. The tactic asks users to comment a specific word to receive a resource via DM, artificially inflating engagement metrics. The author argues this benefits nobody: commenters look foolish, posters still have to manually send DMs, platforms get noise instead of content, and readers can't find meaningful discussion. LinkedIn is called out for rewarding interaction quantity over quality, and the author urges the platform to penalize rather than promote such posts.

recent_posts.title: Quick tip: hosting HTML/CSS/JS demos from source code on GitHub Pages
recent_posts.summary: A quick guide showing how to host live HTML/CSS/JS demos alongside their source code using GitHub Pages. By using Jekyll's `include_relative` tag inside a Markdown file, you can embed and display both the running demo and syntax-highlighted source code in one page. The post walks through forking an example repo, enabling GitHub Pages via repository settings, deploying from the main branch, and monitoring the build via the Actions tab.

recent_posts.title: Five mistakes that led to losing an X account to a phishing attack
recent_posts.summary: A developer with 20 years on Twitter/X shares a personal account of falling for a sophisticated phishing attack that resulted in losing access to their account. The post details five key mistakes: acting in a rush during a security task, not scrutinizing a convincing phishing email, failing to check the sender address or link URL, ignoring the browser autofill not triggering on the fake login form, and not having an authenticator app set up. The attacker quickly changed the account email and locked the victim out. Practical takeaways include always verifying sender and URL, treating missing autofill as a red flag, and using an authenticator app rather than SMS-based 2FA.

recent_posts.title: Developer loses Twitter account access after falling for phishing email
recent_posts.summary: Developer Christian Heilmann shares a brief warning after falling victim to a phishing email that resulted in losing access to his Twitter/X account. He urges followers not to click any links posted from his account and plans to discuss the incident in detail on an upcoming live show, using it as an opportunity to reassess his social media presence.

recent_posts.title: WebMCP gives AI agents structured access to web content instead of scraping
recent_posts.summary: WebMCP is a new W3C proposal that allows web developers to use HTML attributes and JavaScript methods to give AI agents direct access to content, replacing inefficient web scraping. The standard treats agents as first-class web citizens by letting publishers explicitly mark what content agents should access and how to interact with forms programmatically. This approach reduces token consumption for users, prevents wasteful traffic, and returns to the web's original design principle of machine-readable content through semantic HTML, meta tags, and structured data.

recent_posts.title: Monky Business: Creating a Cistercian Numerals Generator
recent_posts.summary: A developer creates a generator for Cistercian numerals, a 13th-century monastic system that represents numbers 1-9999 as single characters. The project includes a web-based generator, a Cistercian clock, and two JavaScript libraries: a simple Node/browser converter that outputs SVG strings, and an advanced version with customization options for SVG, PNG, and Canvas rendering. The implementation uses a coordinate-based approach with a 3x5 grid system and point-connection datasets rather than AI-generated SVG, which initially failed. The code is open-source on GitHub.

recent_posts.title: Stop falling for fear based tech marketing
recent_posts.summary: Fear-based marketing posts claiming you're "already behind" for not adopting specific tools are manipulative and insincere. A successful career doesn't require chasing every trend—Flash, Second Life, blockchain, and other hyped technologies came and went without derailing those who didn't adopt them. Focus on delivering quality work at your own pace rather than reacting to manufactured urgency from thought leaders promoting products.

recent_posts.title: Building my faux lego advent calendar feels like current software development
recent_posts.summary: Building a Blue Brixx advent calendar reveals parallels with modern software development. Like assembling bricks without proper instructions or missing pieces, developers often cobble together libraries and frameworks without full understanding, resulting in bloated, hard-to-maintain solutions. The author advocates for structured planning, proper tooling, documentation, and understanding components before assembly—whether building with bricks or code. The experience highlights how shortcuts and "vibe coding" lead to technical debt, while methodical preparation and documentation create maintainable, repeatable solutions.
